To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a T67A mutation of the proximal pocket high-spin heme in MauG stabilized the mixed-valent Fe(II)/Fe(III) state of the heme and enhanced charge resonance stabilization of bis-FeIV.
the T67A variant of MauG exhibits a mixed-valent heme and that this variant is a more efficient catalyst for TTQ biosynthesis.
the T67A M. barkeri MauG variant has a mixed-valent form, a stabilized charge-resonance transition in the high-valent heme, and an altered proximal pocket of one of its hemes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the structural and functional basis of the redox chemistry of heme-containing proteins, and how the structure of the protein influences its redox chemistry.
the mechanism and function of the diheme MauG enzyme, which is involved in the biosynthesis of tryptophantryptophylquinones.

the role of the high-spin iron in the heme of M. capsulatus MauG in the formation of the high-spin FeIII/FeIV state of the enzyme and the role of the proximal and distal pockets of the high-spin site in stabilization of the high-spin state.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the T67A M. capsulatus MauG mutation affects the proximal pocket, which is consistent with the location of the residue, and that the effects of the mutation are not due to the presence of a second heme.
the T67A variant is a mixed-valent enzyme with a bis-FeII/FeIII heme that has enhanced stabilization of its charge-resonance transition.
the proximal and distal heme environments of MauG have different roles in controlling the reactivity of the high-spin and low-spin heme sites.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the proximal pocket is more important than the distal pocket in the stabilization of the high-spin FeIV state of MauG.
the proximal pocket plays a role in the redox properties of the low- and high-spin hemes and in the stabilization of the high valence state of MauG.
the proximal and distal environments of the high-spin and low-spin hemes are both required for optimal electron transfer and charge resonance stabilization of MauG.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single amino acid residue in the proximal heme pocket can influence the redox and electronic properties of the heme cofactors of MauG.
the proximal pocket residues of the high-spin MauG heme are important for the redox chemistry of the protein.
mutations that affect the redox and charge resonance transition properties of the hemes of MauG are not necessarily deleterious to the function of this enzyme.
